summary: Lights at the Mispillion River mouth since 1831; the 1873 wooden house burned in 2002 and was rebuilt in Lewes.

lens.where: 1873 tower; sixth-order lens first shown June 1873 (LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: Built at Cape Henlopen about 1924; re-erected at Mispillion in 1929. Nomination: 60 feet.

access.note: The 1873 house stands in Shipcarpenter Square, Lewes, a neighborhood reserved for residences; it can be viewed from Burton Avenue. The former station site is by the DuPont Nature Center. Do not enter the private property.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (steel beacon, per the 1986 nomination)

events.note: Lantern with six lamps set atop the keeper's dwelling; completed by October 19, 1831

New light built in the same configuration as the 1831 building (LighthouseFriends); the Slaughter Beach Historical Society also dates a rebuild to 1839 after inspections. The nomination does not mention it.
Light discontinued; building sold for $135 and moved to Milford, where it became a storehouse
Third structure lit June 15, 1873 (LighthouseFriends); the Slaughter Beach Historical Society dates the lighting to June 27, 1873
Acetylene lighting system; keeper post ended; caretaker at $60 a year
Steel skeletal beacon from Cape Henlopen re-erected at Mispillion
Lighthouse and most of the station sold by the federal government for $400 to two local businessmen
Steel beacon deactivated by the Coast Guard
Sold, along with a restaurant and marina, to a private couple
Bought by a local lawyer, Merritt Burke III, who had planned to work with a non-profit
Struck by lightning on May 2, 2002; the upper tower and much of the interior burned
Remains removed to an undisclosed location, later Shipcarpenter Square, Lewes
Burke family sold the site to the State of Delaware for $1.2 million (LighthouseFriends note)
Reconstructed and expanded house in Shipcarpenter Square; modern lantern placed in July 2005
Iron tower that replaced the lighthouse removed (LighthouseFriends). Disputed: see notes_for_editor.

corrections.why: The record's point (LighthouseFriends) is about 22 km south-east, in Delaware Bay near Slaughter Beach, and LighthouseFriends itself says the light was 'formerly located at the mouth of the Mispillion River, north of Slaughter Beach'. The 1986 nomination places the station at the north-east end of County Road 203, where Cedar Creek and the Mispillion River join, near Milford. USLHS's 'Mispillion New' place record (established 1873) gives latitude 38 56.49' and longitude 75 18.57' (38.9415, -75.3095).

corrections.proposed: wooden integral tower built 1873, 19.8 m (65 ft); steel skeletal beacon built about 1924 at Cape Henlopen, re-erected here 1929, 18.3 m (60 ft)
corrections.why: The 1873 tower is wood (nomination sections 7 and 8). The steel tower was built at Cape Henlopen about 1924 and moved here in 1929 (nomination section 8). Two different structures are merged in the record.
The nomination says the 1911 acetylene system made the keeper's post unnecessary. No source read supports 1926 for automation.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's conflict over the year the light went out is two different structures: the 1831/1839 light was deactivated in 1859, and the 1873 wooden light in 1929 (the steel beacon followed until 1984). The sources agree on each date.
The nomination and LighthouseFriends agree the 1873 building was wooden with a square tower, about 65 feet overall; the steel beacon was a separate structure from Cape Henlopen.

notes_for_editor: 1) Sources disagree on the 1873 lighting day: LighthouseFriends says June 15, the Slaughter Beach Historical Society June 27 (both in the story). 2) The 1874 money: a letter to the editor printed in the Wilmington Daily Gazette (Oct 28, 1874, 'Now, Mr. Editor'; the writer's name is not legible in the OCR) says the $5,000 was a keeper's dwelling and that the member's only effort was that appropriation 'as I understand'; LighthouseFriends says a cistern and four rooms. The story states both and does not take the letter as a record. 3) The steel beacon's fate is unresolved: LighthouseFriends says removed in 2016 but an undated note on the page says the skeletal tower still remains; the 1986 nomination describes it as federal property, not its condition. Needs a field check or a DNREC answer. Wikipedia (not cited) says demolished 2008. 4) Keepers are the USLHS roster (NARA register inventory per the archive). The tool asks that each keeper be confirmed in a primary record before naming; I did not confirm them in the Official Register or the NARA registers. The archive files the 1873 light's keepers under the 'Mispillion (Old)' place. 5) The 1857 Light-House Board passage is taken from LighthouseFriends; the 1857 report is not in the local corpus (it holds Lighthouse Board volumes for 1891-1901 only). 6) The record's position (38.776648, -75.145565) is LighthouseFriends' and places the light about 22 km from the USLHS and NRHP location; see corrections. 7) USCG Historian page (history.uscg.mil, Mispillion Lighthouse) could not be read: the Wayback captures returned only the wrapper or 403, so the 1839/1857 date discrepancy the search snippet mentions is unverified here. 8) Record items not sourced here and left out of facts: characteristic 'Fl W 3s' (only Wikipedia gives it), the 1831 tower of 11.6 m, the 1926 automation date, and the NRHP listing date (1987), which I did not check in NPGallery's record. 9) Milford Chronicle, 12 May 1933, names two purchasers (W. V. Benson and G. C. Bridham) and mentions a family living in the buildings; the story names the purchasers in their public role and leaves the family out. 10) Milford Chronicle pages for 1929 that I checked had no lighthouse content. 11) No wreck or rescue at the station itself was found in the sources read; the story therefore has none beyond the ice, fog and fire items. 12) The second Mispillion record (us-de-mispillion-2) is already merged into this one; no action. 13) The archive's 'Open to Public: No' flag refers to the 1873 place record and may not describe the present steel beacon. 14) Fixed in the 2026-10-28 check: the opening no longer states the 1839 rebuild as settled; LighthouseFriends and the SBHS give it, and the nomination says only that the first light fell to erosion. 15) The 1912 fog story now follows the Milford Chronicle's order: the outbound trip went wrong in the bay with no fog mentioned, and the fog came on the homeward leg.
